questions.q: Why does the lesson say 'being right' is necessary but no longer sufficient as the senior-most technical voice in a room?
options: There is no real difference between being right as a mid-level engineer and as a senior one
Senior engineers are never actually right more often than junior engineers
Being right stops mattering entirely once you reach a senior role
If the room doesn't understand why or doesn't feel ownership over a correct decision, that decision erodes once the senior person isn't there to defend it, and the team's own judgment never develops
questions.explain: A correct answer the room doesn't understand or own is fragile -- it holds only while the senior person is present to keep defending it, which is a different, weaker outcome than a decision the room reasoned its way into.

questions.q: What is the specific behavior shift the lesson describes as 'the senior move'?
options: Always providing the answer immediately, as fast as possible, in every single meeting
Shifting from directly supplying the answer to shaping how the room reaches a good answer itself, through better questions rather than handed-down conclusions
Refusing to ever share technical knowledge with the team under any circumstances
Deferring every single technical decision to the most junior person in the room
questions.explain: The shift is from 'here's the answer' to 'here's the question we should be asking' -- redirecting the room's reasoning rather than shortcutting it, so the room ends up owning the conclusion.

questions.q: What is the real, longer-term cost of a senior engineer answering every question fastest in every meeting, even when every individual answer is correct?
options: This habit only affects the senior engineer's own performance, never the team's
There is no real cost -- faster correct answers are always strictly better for the team
The senior engineer's answers become less accurate over time as a direct result
The team quietly learns that waiting for the senior engineer is more efficient than thinking it through themselves, and the team's collective judgment never gets exercised or developed
questions.explain: This is the chapter's named failure mode -- reflexive deference develops quietly, and the team's own decision-making capability erodes from simply never being used, even though each individual interaction looked helpful.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what reveals that a team was never actually making its own decisions, but relying entirely on one senior engineer?
options: The team suddenly struggles to make decisions it used to make easily, once that senior engineer leaves (promotion, new project, new company)
The team's decisions get noticeably better immediately after the senior engineer leaves
The team starts making faster decisions once the senior engineer is no longer present
This situation never actually happens in real engineering teams
questions.explain: A team that suddenly can't make a decision it used to make easily reveals that the senior engineer, not the team, was actually making it all along -- the team's apparent competence was borrowed, not developed.

questions.q: When does the lesson say it's actually fine, even correct, for a senior engineer to just give a direct answer?
options: Only when the entire team is in agreement already before the question is asked
A senior engineer should never under any circumstances give a direct answer
When the question is a genuine knowledge gap only the senior person has (a specific factual answer), as opposed to a judgment call the team is capable of reasoning through themselves
Only during performance reviews, never during regular technical meetings
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly distinguishes a factual knowledge gap (fine to just answer) from a reasoning/judgment call the team could work through themselves (better served by facilitating) -- not a blanket rule against ever answering directly.
